GHMR SAFE OPERATIONAL
PLAN FOR BUTANE
TRANSLOAD.
This comprehensive operational plan establishes GHMR's safety protocols,
procedures, and responsibilities for the transloading of butane gas from
railcar tanks to 18-wheeler trucks. The document outlines GHMR's regulatory
compliance requirements, personnel qualifications, equipment specifications,
emergency response procedures, and continuous improvement processes to
ensure safe and efficient operations while minimizing environmental impact
and risk to personnel.
Scope of Operations
This plan covers butane transfer activities at the GHMR facility. it includes moving butane from DOT-112 and DOT-114
railcar tanks to MC-331 trucks. This plan does not cover fixed facilities or other products.
Site Location
Transfer operations take place at
the GHMR Rail Terminal located in:
1485 Texas Gulf Plant Rd Fort
Stockton, TX 79735
Operational Period
Transfer is allowed 12 hours a day,
6 days a week, with proper staffing
and good weather. Night
operations need special Class I,
Division 1 lighting per NFPA 70.
Operations must stop during
lightning, winds over 30 mph, or
when temperatures are below
-20°F or above 120°F.
Equipment Capacity
This plan covers handling up to 6
railcars and 12 trucks daily. Each
railcar typically holds 30,000
gallons of butane, while each truck
holds about 11,500 gallons,
requiring multiple trucks per
railcar.
Operations include railcar positioning, inspection, connecting equipment, equalizing pressure, transferring product,
disconnecting, and post-transfer steps. Each step has specific safety rules that all workers must follow. This plan does not
cover maintenance on the railcars or trucks, which must be done by qualified workers under different protocols.
All transfer activities must be recorded as required in Section 13 of this plan. Any changes to this scope need management
approval and possible updates to this plan before starting.
Regulatory and Compliance Requirements
Butane transloading operations

must comply with numerous federal, state, and local regulations to ensure safety,
environmental protection, and legal compliance. This section outlines the key regulatory frameworks that govern these
operations.
Regulatory Body Regulation Key Requirements
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.110 Storage and handling of LP gases,
training requirements, PPE
specifications
DOT 49 CFR Parts 171-180 Hazardous materials transportation,
packaging, and container
specifications
EPA 40 CFR Part 68 Risk Management Program for
chemical accident prevention
NFPA NFPA 58 Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code for
safe handling and storage
State of Texas Texas Administrative Code, Title 16,
Part 1, Chapter 14
State-specific requirements for LPgas
operations
Permits and Licenses
Operations require a valid
Hazardous Materials Transfer
Permit (Form HM-126) issued
by the local fire marshal,
renewed annually. All operators
must maintain applicable
commercial driver's licenses
with HAZMAT endorsements.
Site must maintain an EPA
Facility ID under the Risk
Management Program if
quantities exceed threshold
amounts.
Reporting Obligations
Any spill exceeding 10 gallons
of liquid butane must be
reported to the National
Response Center (1-800-424-
8802) within 15 minutes.
Releases exceeding reportable
quantities must also be
reported to state emergency
response commission and local
emergency planning committee
per EPCRA requirements.
Documentation
Requirements
Daily inspection logs, transfer
manifests, training records, and
incident reports must be
maintained on-site for a
minimum of 3 years. Safety
Data Sheets must be readily
accessible to all personnel.
DOT shipping papers must
accompany each shipment and
be properly transferred between
responsible parties.
The GHMR facility must conduct quarterly compliance audits to verify adherence to these regulations. Any compliance
deficiencies must be documented and addressed through a formal corrective action process. The Site Supervisor is
responsible for maintaining a current li

brary of all applicable regulations and ensuring that any regulatory changes are
promptly incorporated into operational procedures.
In addition to the federal requirements, the GHMR facility must adhere to Texas Commission on Environmental Quality
(TCEQ) air quality regulations regarding vapor emissions during transfer operations. This includes maintaining vapor
recovery equipment, conducting regular leak detection and repair (LDAR) inspections, and submitting annual emissions
inventories to regulatory authorities. Failure to comply with any of these requirements may result in regulatory penalties,
operational shutdowns, or revocation of permits.
Definitions and Terminology
To ensure clarity and consistent understanding throughout this GHMR operational plan, the following key terms and
definitions are established. Proper understanding of these terms is critical for all personnel involved in GHMR butane
transloading operations.
Key Operational Terms
Butane: Highly flammable, colorless hydrocarbon gas
(C¤H¡ ) that liquefies under pressure
Loading Arm: Articulated pipe system used to connect
the GHMR transloader to railcars or trucks
Vapor Recovery: System designed to capture and
recover butane vapors during GHMR transfer
operations
Bonding: The process of connecting two or more
objects with an electrical conductor to equalize
potential difference
Grounding: The practice of connecting equipment to
earth to prevent static electricity buildup
Safety and Regulatory Terms
PPE: Personal Protective Equipment required for
GHMR worker safety
Exclusion Zone: Designated safety perimeter (100 ft
radius) around GHMR transloading operations
LEL: Lower Explosive Limit, minimum concentration
needed for ignition
SDS: Safety Data Sheet containing information on
chemical hazards
Hot Work: Any operation involving open flames or
producing heat/sparks
Lockout/Tagout: Procedure to disable machinery
during maintenance
This GHMR operational plan references and adheres to standards established

by the following organizations: National Fire
Protection Association (NFPA) Standards 58 and 30; Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) 29 CFR
1910.110; American Petroleum Institute (API) RP 2003; and Department of Transportation (DOT) 49 CFR Parts 171-180.
GHMR personnel must familiarize themselves with these references as they contain critical safety information applicable to
transloading operations.
All measurements, pressures, and specifications referenced in this GHMR document use standard units as specified in the
referenced standards. GHMR personnel must be proficient in reading and interpreting these measurements on equipment
gauges, testing instruments, and documentation.
Roles and Responsibilities
Effective GHMR butane transloading operations require clearly defined roles with specific responsibilities assigned to
qualified personnel. This section outlines the key positions involved in the GHMR transloading process and their respective
duties.
GHMR Site Supervisor
Maintains overall responsibility for site safety and regulatory compliance
Authorizes daily operations based on weather conditions and personnel availability
Serves as Incident Commander during emergency situations
Reviews and approves all documentation prior to beginning transloading operations
Conducts pre-shift safety briefings and ensures all personnel understand their duties
Has authority to suspend operations for safety concerns without higher approval
GHMR Transloading Operators (minimum of 2 required)
Conducts physical inspection of all equipment prior to operation
Operates the GHMR mobile transloader system according to standard procedures
Monitors pressure gauges, flow rates, and equipment during transfers
Manages connections between railcars, transloader, and trucks
Performs regular gas detection testing throughout operations
Maintains continuous communication with GHMR Site Supervisor and other personnel
GHMR Safety Officer
Ensures compliance with all safety protocols a

nd regulatory requirements
Conducts regular safety audits and inspections of equipment and procedures
Verifies proper PPE usage by all personnel in the operational area
Maintains and calibrates gas detection and emergency response equipment
Leads training on emergency response procedures and equipment
Has parallel authority with GHMR Site Supervisor to halt operations for safety concerns
Third-Party Drivers
Completes mandatory GHMR site safety orientation before entering facility
Provides proper documentation for vehicles and HAZMAT endorsements
Positions trucks according to GHMR Site Supervisor's direction
Remains in designated safe area during active transloading
Performs pre- and post-transfer truck inspections
Complies with all GHMR site rules regarding smoking, electronic devices, and PPE
Additionally, the GHMR Control Room Operator maintains oversight of site operations from a safe distance, monitoring
weather conditions, coordinating communications, and activating emergency response systems when necessary. During
night operations, a dedicated GHMR Fire Watch must be assigned to monitor for potential ignition sources or leaks.
All GHMR personnel share the responsibility to stop operations immediately if unsafe conditions are observed, regardless
of their position. The GHMR "Stop Work Authority" policy empowers every individual to halt operations without fear of
reprisal when safety concerns arise. Communication between all roles is maintained via intrinsically safe two-way radios
operating on designated GHMR frequencies.
During shift changes, a formal transfer of responsibility must occur with the outgoing and incoming GHMR personnel
conducting a joint inspection and status briefing. This transfer must be documented on the GHMR Shift Handover form and
signed by both parties before the outgoing personnel leave the site.
Personnel Qualifications and Training
All personnel involved in butane transloading operations must possess specific qualifications and undergo

comprehensive
training before being authorized to perform their duties. This section outlines the minimum requirements for personnel
certification, training programs, and ongoing competency verification.
Required Certifications
All operational personnel must hold current
certifications in HAZMAT handling (per 49 CFR
172.704), OSHA HAZWOPER 24-hour training,
confined space entry procedures, fire extinguisher
use, and first aid/CPR. Fork truck operators must
possess valid powered industrial truck certification.
Site Supervisors must additionally hold Incident
Command System (ICS) certification at the ICS-300
level.
Initial Training Program
New personnel must complete a 40-hour
comprehensive training program covering:
properties of butane, equipment operation, leak
detection, emergency procedures, personal
protective equipment, documentation requirements,
and site-specific hazards. This training includes both
classroom instruction and supervised hands-on
practice with inert materials before progressing to
live operations.
Refresher Training
All personnel must complete annual 8-hour refresher
training covering regulatory updates, procedure
modifications, lessons learned from incidents, and
hands-on equipment operation validation. Additional
specialized training is required whenever new
equipment or procedures are introduced to the
operation.
Emergency Response Drills
Quarterly emergency response drills must be
conducted to practice procedures for: butane
releases, fires, medical emergencies, extreme
weather events, and security incidents. These drills
include coordination with local emergency
responders and must be documented with afteraction
reviews to identify improvement
opportunities.
Job Hazard Analysis and Competency Verification
Prior to independent work, each employee must participate in a detailed Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) for their specific role,
identifying potential hazards and appropriate mitigation measures. Competency must be verified through written
exa

minations (minimum passing score of 80%) and practical demonstrations observed by qualified evaluators. Reverification
is required annually or after any significant procedure change.
Third-Party Contractor Requirements
Contractors, including truck drivers, must complete a site-specific orientation program covering emergency procedures,
communication protocols, and site hazards before being granted access to operational areas. The orientation includes
verification of required DOT HAZMAT endorsements and review of company-specific safety policies. Contractor training
records must be maintained on file at the GHMR facility.
All training activities must be documented in the company's Learning Management System with electronic records
maintained for a minimum of 5 years. These records are subject to regulatory inspection and must include: dates, duration,
topics covered, instructor qualifications, attendance verification, and competency assessment results. The Training
Coordinator conducts quarterly audits of all personnel records to ensure compliance with qualification requirements and to
schedule upcoming refresher training as needed.
Site Preparation and Control
Proper site preparation and control are critical elements for maintaining safe butane transloading operations at GHMR
facilities. This section details the requirements for establishing operational boundaries, controlling access, evaluating
environmental conditions, and implementing ignition source controls.
Exclusion Zone Establishment
A minimum 100-foot radius exclusion zone must be
established around all active GHMR transloading
operations. This zone must be clearly marked with
red safety tape, cones, and signage reading
"DANGER - HAZARDOUS AREA - AUTHORIZED
PERSONNEL ONLY". During night operations, the
perimeter must be illuminated with intrinsically safe
lighting. Only essential GHMR personnel wearing
appropriate PPE are permitted within this zone
during active operations.
Access Control
Entry to the GHMR

transloading area requires checkin
at the security gate, verification of training
credentials, and issuance of a visible identification
badge. A Personnel Tracking Board must be
maintained showing all individuals currently within
the operational area. Vehicle access is restricted to
essential equipment only, with designated parking
areas located outside the exclusion zone. Visitors
must be escorted at all times and receive a GHMR
safety briefing before entry.
Traffic Management
A Traffic Control Plan must be implemented with
designated routes for truck approach, queuing,
loading, and departure. Maximum speed limit within
the GHMR facility is 5 mph with clearly posted
signage. Trucks must be guided by spotters when
backing or positioning for loading. Railway derailers
must be installed on both ends of the loading track
to prevent unexpected railcar movement during
operations.
Environmental Assessment
Prior to commencing operations, the GHMR Site
Supervisor must conduct an environmental
assessment including wind direction (using
windsocks positioned at multiple locations),
precipitation probability, lightning risk, and
temperature conditions. Operations must be
suspended during electrical storms within 10 miles,
winds exceeding 30 mph, or when ambient
temperatures fall outside equipment operating
parameters (-20°F to 120°F).
Ignition Source Control
All equipment within the exclusion zone must be intrinsically safe and rated for Class I Division 1 Group D hazardous
locations per NFPA 70. A comprehensive ignition source assessment must be conducted prior to GHMR operations,
including verification that:
No smoking, open flames, or hot work is permitted within 100 feet of operations
All vehicles in the vicinity have engines shut off during transfer operations
Non-intrinsically safe electronics (including cell phones) are prohibited in the exclusion zone
All equipment is properly bonded and grounded to prevent static electricity buildup
Tools used in the area must be non-s

parking (brass, aluminum bronze, or beryllium copper)
Before each operational shift, the GHMR Safety Officer must verify and document that all site preparation requirements
have been properly implemented using the GHMR Site Readiness Checklist (Form SRC-101). Any deficiencies must be
corrected before transloading operations can begin. The exclusion zone must be continuously monitored for unauthorized
personnel or potential hazards throughout the duration of operations.
In the event of a site control breach or deteriorating environmental conditions, the GHMR Site Supervisor has the authority
and responsibility to immediately halt operations until safe conditions can be restored. A comprehensive site inspection
must be completed after any interruption before operations can resume.
Equipment and Materials
The GHMR mobile transloader system is designed
specifically for safe butane transfer operations with
integrated safety features including emergency shutdown
systems, pressure relief valves, and continuous monitoring
capabilities.
Mobile Transloader Specifications
The primary transloading system consists of a skidmounted
TranSafe 5000 unit with the following
specifications:
Maximum flow rate: 250 gallons per minute
Operating pressure range: 50-375 psig
3-inch schedule 80 stainless steel piping with 600#
ANSI flanges
Explosion-proof electric motor with Class I Div 1 rating
Interlocked emergency shutdown system with remote
activation
Integrated vapor recovery system with compressor
Anti-static conveyor belt with conductive path to
ground
Self-contained hydraulic positioning system
Connection Systems
All hose assemblies must meet the following requirements:
Stainless steel braided hoses with 3-inch internal diameter rated for LPG service
Working pressure rating of minimum 350 psig with 4:1 safety factor
Maximum length of 15 feet to minimize potential leak points
Equipped with dry-break quick disconnect couplings and check valves
Tested and certified annually with document

ation tags attached
Inspected visually before each use for damage or deterioration
Inspection Protocols
Equipment inspection schedules
are as follows:
Pre-operational inspection
before each shift using
checklist EQ-101
Weekly comprehensive
inspection of all components
Monthly third-party inspection
of critical safety systems
Quarterly pressure testing of all
transfer hoses
Annual certification of
pressure relief devices
Emergency Equipment
The following emergency
equipment must be maintained at
the transloading location:
Two 150-lb wheeled dry
chemical fire extinguishers
(Purple K)
Emergency response kit with
absorbent materials
First aid station with
emergency eye wash
Wind socks positioned at
multiple locations
Emergency shutdown controls
at four strategic positions
Personal Protective
Equipment
Required PPE for all personnel in
the exclusion zone:
Flame-resistant clothing
meeting NFPA 2112 standards
Safety glasses with side
shields and face shields
Hard hats with flame-resistant
liners
Leather gloves for mechanical
protection
Static-dissipative safety
footwear
Personal LEL/O¢/H¢S gas
monitors calibrated monthly
All equipment must be maintained according to manufacturer's specifications and industry best practices. Maintenance
records must be kept on file for a minimum of three years and made available during regulatory inspections. Spare parts
inventory must include critical components such as gaskets, valve seats, and emergency shutdown system parts to
minimize downtime during essential repairs.
Equipment that fails inspection or becomes damaged during operations must be immediately tagged out of service using
the company's Lockout/Tagout procedure and replaced with certified equipment before operations can continue. Repairs to
safety-critical systems must be validated by qualified technicians and documented before the equipment can be returned
to service.
Pre-Operational Safety Checks
Comprehensive pre-operational safety checks are essential to ensure all equip

ment is functioning properly and hazards are
controlled before beginning butane transloading operations. This section details the required inspections, verifications, and
authorizations that must be completed prior to any transfer activities.
Documentation Review
The Site Supervisor must verify all required
documentation is current and available, including:
Transfer permits and regulatory authorizations
Safety Data Sheets for butane
Personnel training certifications
Equipment inspection and testing records
Pre-work risk assessment
Emergency response plan with current contact
information
Railcar Inspection
Operators must conduct a detailed inspection of
each railcar using Checklist RC-101, verifying:
DOT specification markings and test date
currency
Absence of physical damage or leaks around
valves and fittings
Proper positioning and securement with wheel
chocks and derailers
Pressure gauge readings within acceptable
range (50-175 psig)
Proper product identification and hazard
placards
Functional pressure relief valves without
tampering evidence
Truck Inspection
Each truck must be inspected using Checklist TR-
102, confirming:
Current DOT inspection and pressure test
certifications
Proper MC-331 specification compliance
Working emergency shutdown systems
Functional brake interlocks
Proper grounding connection points
Capacity verification for planned transfer
volume
Transfer Equipment Preparation
The transloading system must be prepared
according to Procedure TE-103:
Visual inspection of all hoses, gaskets, and
connections
Verification of emergency shutdown system
functionality
Pressure testing of transfer lines with nitrogen
at 1.5x operating pressure
Positioning and secure anchoring of the
transloader unit
Establishment of bonding and grounding
connections with verification of continuity
(resistance less than 10 ohms)
Verification that all valves are in the correct
starting position
Safety Systems Verification
Before operations commence, the Safety Officer must veri

fy and document the following items using Safety Verification
Form SV-104:
1 Gas Detection
Calibration check of all fixed and portable gas
detectors with test gas. Alarms must be set to
activate at 10% of LEL for butane. A minimum of
four portable gas detectors must be distributed
throughout the operational area with operators
trained in their use.
2 Fire Suppression
Confirmation that all required fire extinguishing
equipment is in place, accessible, and fully charged.
Fire monitors must be positioned to cover the
transfer area and tested for proper operation. Water
supply for fire suppression must be verified as
operational with adequate pressure.
3 Communication Systems
Testing of all two-way radios on the designated
emergency channel. Verification of backup
communication systems including air horns for
emergency evacuation signals. Confirmation that all
personnel understand emergency communication
protocols.
4 Permits and Authorizations
Final review and sign-off on all required permits
including hot work exclusions, confined space
prohibitions, and work authorizations. The Safety
Officer and Site Supervisor must both sign the
Master Transfer Authorization form before
operations can commence.
Upon completion of all pre-operational checks, a mandatory safety briefing must be conducted with all personnel involved
in the transfer operation. This briefing must cover hazards specific to the day's operations, weather considerations,
emergency response procedures, and individual responsibilities. All participants must sign the briefing acknowledgment
form before assuming their duties.
Any deficiencies identified during pre-operational checks must be corrected and re-verified before transfer operations can
begin. The authority to commence operations rests jointly with the Site Supervisor and Safety Officer, with either individual
having full authority to delay or cancel operations if safety concerns cannot be adequately addressed.
Standard Operating Procedures for
Translo

ading
This section outlines the systematic process for safely transferring butane from railcars to trucks using the mobile
transloader system. Each step must be performed in the prescribed sequence by qualified personnel, with continuous
monitoring throughout the operation.
Preparation Phase
Establish exclusion zone,
position equipment, and
complete all preoperational
checks per
Section 9.
Connection Phase
Establish proper
connections between
railcar, transloader, and
truck with verification.
Transfer Phase
Control product flow
through systematic valve
operation and continuous
monitoring.
Disconnection
Phase
Safely terminate transfer,
depressurize lines, and
disconnect equipment.
Detailed Transfer Procedure
Initial Position Verification: Confirm railcar handbrake is set, wheels are chocked, derailers are in place, and truck is
properly positioned with engine off and brake interlocks engaged.
1.
Bonding and Grounding: Connect grounding cables to designated points on railcar, transloader, and truck. Verify
continuity with testing meter (must read less than 10 ohms). All connections must be made before any product valves
are opened.
2.
3. Connection Sequence:
All connections must use new gaskets and be tightened to proper torque specifications.
Connect vapor line from transloader to railcar vapor valve
Connect liquid line from transloader to railcar liquid valve
Connect vapor line from transloader to truck vapor valve
Connect liquid line from transloader to truck liquid valve
Pressure Equalization: Slowly open vapor valves to equalize pressure between containers. Monitor pressure gauges
continuously during this process. If pressure differential exceeds 15 psig, slow the equalization process.
1.
2. Transfer Initiation:
Confirm all monitoring systems are operational
Slowly open liquid valves on railcar side
Start transloader pump at minimum flow rate (50 GPM)
Open liquid valves on truck side
Gradually increase to target flow rate (not to exceed 200 GPM)
Continuous Monito

ring Requirements
Throughout the transfer process, operators must
continuously monitor:
Pressure gauges on railcar, transloader, and truck
(maximum operating pressure: 375 psig)
Flow rate indicators (target: 150-200 GPM)
Leak detection using portable gas monitors around all
connection points
Temperature of product and equipment (maximum:
100°F)
Unusual noises, vibrations, or other signs of
mechanical problems
Truck capacity to prevent overfilling (maximum fill: 85%
of water capacity)
Weather conditions, particularly wind direction and
lightning proximity
Transfer Termination Procedure
Shut down transloader pump when truck reaches
target volume
1.
2. Close liquid valve on railcar side
3. Allow remaining liquid in lines to flow into truck
4. Close liquid valve on truck side
Slowly depressurize transfer lines using bleeder valves
(direct to vapor recovery)
5.
6. Close vapor valves on both railcar and truck
Verify zero pressure in transfer lines before
disconnection
7.
8. Disconnect lines in reverse order of connection
9. Cap all openings immediately after disconnection
Documentation Requirements
The following documentation must be completed for each transfer operation:
Pre-transfer inspection forms for railcar and truck
Transfer log recording start time, completion time, volumes, pressures, and temperatures
Bill of lading with proper DOT shipping description
Equipment monitoring log with readings taken at 15-minute intervals
Post-transfer inspection verifying all valves are closed and secured
Any deviation from these procedures requires immediate cessation of transfer activities and notification of the Site
Supervisor. Operations may only resume after the situation has been evaluated and deemed safe by both the Site
Supervisor and Safety Officer. All incidents, including near-misses, must be documented and reported according to Section
13 of this plan.
Emergency Response and Spill Control
Effective emergency response is critical for minimizing the consequences of incid

ents during butane transloading
operations. This section outlines the procedures for identifying, reporting, and responding to emergencies, with an
emphasis on butane releases, fires, and personnel injuries.
Emergency Classification
Emergencies are classified into three levels to determine appropriate response actions:
Level Description Examples Response
Level 1 Minor incident
containable by on-site
personnel
Small leak at connection
point, minor equipment
failure
On-site response team
only
Level 2 Moderate incident
requiring additional
resources
Significant butane
release, small fire, injury
requiring medical
attention
On-site team plus local
emergency services
Level 3 Major incident with
potential off-site impact
Large release with vapor
cloud, uncontrolled fire,
multiple injuries
Full emergency response,
potential evacuation of
surrounding area
Emergency Detection and
Alarm
Emergencies may be detected through
gas monitors, visual observation,
equipment alarms, or personnel
reports. Upon detection of an
emergency condition, the alarm must
be raised immediately by: activating
the nearest emergency alarm pull
station, using radio communication
(declaring "Emergency, Emergency,
Emergency" followed by location and
nature), or using the site air horn
system (three long blasts). All nonessential
operations must cease
immediately when an alarm is
activated.
Initial Response Actions
The first person to discover an
emergency must: ensure personal
safety first, activate the alarm system,
notify the Site Supervisor with
essential information (location, nature
of emergency, persons involved,
actions taken), control the incident if it
is safe to do so using emergency
equipment, and guide emergency
responders to the location. The Site
Supervisor assumes the role of
Incident Commander until relieved by
higher authority or emergency
services.
Evacuation Procedures
When evacuation is necessary, all
personnel must: stop work
immediately, shut down equipment if
possible without risk

ing safety,
proceed to the nearest safe exit
upwind of the incident, report to the
designated assembly area (northeast
corner of parking area), check in with
the Personnel Accountability
Coordinator, and remain at the
assembly area until authorized to
leave. Primary and secondary
evacuation routes are posted
throughout the facility and included in
site orientation materials.
Butane Release Response
In the event of a butane release, the following specific actions must be taken:
1 Isolation
Stop the flow of product if possible by closing the
nearest upstream valve. Eliminate all ignition
sources in the area. Establish an expanded exclusion
zone (minimum 300 feet for significant releases)
and restrict access. Position responders upwind of
the release.
2 Containment
Liquid butane releases should be contained using
the site's secondary containment systems. Prevent
liquid from entering drains or waterways. For vapor
releases, use water fog (not straight streams) to
direct vapors away from ignition sources and
populated areas.
3 Monitoring
Deploy gas detection equipment to establish the
perimeter of the hazardous atmosphere (25% LEL
boundary). Monitor wind direction continuously to
adjust evacuation zones as needed. Conduct air
monitoring at the facility boundary to determine
potential off-site impacts.
4 Notification
For reportable releases (more than 10 gallons liquid),
notify: National Response Center (1-800-424-8802),
State Emergency Response Commission, Local
Emergency Planning Committee, and corporate
incident management team. Provide location,
material, quantity, time, containment status, and
callback information.
Fire Response
Butane fires should only be extinguished if the source of fuel can be stopped. Otherwise, protect exposures and allow to
burn under controlled conditions. The site's fire suppression strategy includes:
Use of Class B fire extinguishing agents (dry chemical, CO¢) for small fires
Application of water to cool exposed containers and prevent BLEVE

(Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion)
Coordination with local fire department through pre-established response plans
Defensive operations to prevent fire spread until specialized resources arrive
All emergency response actions must be documented in detail including: timeline of events, personnel involved, actions
taken, resources used, and effectiveness of response. A formal incident investigation must be conducted for all Level 2 and
Level 3 emergencies, with findings incorporated into training and procedural improvements. Emergency response
equipment must be inspected and restocked immediately following any incident to ensure readiness for subsequent
events.
Environmental Protection Measures
Environmental Impact Overview
Butane transloading operations present several potential
environmental impacts that must be actively managed. As
a volatile organic compound (VOC), butane can contribute
to air quality issues if released. While it does not present
significant water or soil contamination concerns due to
rapid vaporization, the GHMR facility implements
comprehensive measures to minimize all potential
environmental impacts in accordance with EPA regulations
and corporate environmental stewardship principles.
Air Quality Management
Vapor Recovery System
The transloading operation utilizes
a closed-loop vapor recovery
system that captures displaced
vapors during transfers. The
system includes:
Vapor balance lines connecting
railcars and trucks
Vapor compression unit for
recovery of product
Pressure monitoring to ensure
system integrity
Leak Detection and Repair
(LDAR) program with quarterly
monitoring
Emissions Monitoring
The facility maintains a
comprehensive air monitoring
program:
Fixed LEL monitors at strategic
locations around the transfer
area
Quarterly emissions inventory
calculations
Annual third-party verification
of emissions data
Continuous improvement
targets for emissions reduction
Transfer Efficiency
Operational practices designed to
minimize emissi

ons include:
Dry-break connections to
minimize product loss during
coupling/uncoupling
Controlled flow rates to reduce
turbulence and vapor
generation
Scheduled transfers during
favorable atmospheric
conditions
Regular maintenance to
minimize leaks from valves
and fittings
Spill Prevention and Containment
Although liquid butane rapidly vaporizes when released, the facility implements robust spill prevention measures:
The transloading area features an impervious concrete pad with containment curbing capable of holding 110% of the
largest container volume
All transfer connections occur within the containment area
Storm water from the containment area passes through a monitoring system before discharge
Spill control materials, including specialized foam for vapor suppression, are maintained in accessible locations
The site Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) includes specific provisions for butane transloading operations
Waste Management
The transloading operation generates minimal waste, but all materials are managed according to applicable regulations:
Used gaskets and seals are collected in designated containers and disposed of as industrial waste
Any contaminated water from containment areas is collected and properly disposed of by licensed contractors
Maintenance waste (lubricants, filters) is managed according to the facility's waste management program
Recycling programs are in place for packaging materials and office waste
Environmental Incident Response
In the event of an environmental release:
1. The release must be immediately reported to the Site Supervisor and Safety Officer
If the release exceeds reportable quantities (100 pounds for butane), notifications must be made to appropriate
regulatory agencies
2.
3. Air monitoring must be conducted to determine the extent of the vapor plume
4. An incident investigation must identify root causes and corrective actions
5. Environmental incidents must be tracked and trended as part of the environmental mana

gement system
The facility maintains an Environmental Management System (EMS) aligned with ISO 14001 standards. Annual
environmental objectives and targets are established to drive continuous improvement in environmental performance. All

Documentation Management System
We manage all documents through the Vista Document Control System, which includes:
Central digital storage with security controls
Standard document format and numbering
Revision control with approval steps
Automatic alerts when documents expire
Record of who accessed or changed documents
Weekly backups stored off-site
Record Retention and Accessibility
We follow a Records Retention Schedule that shows how long to keep each type of document. Important records are kept
in two places 3 one digital copy and one paper copy in a fireproof cabinet. Records must be available to:
Staff who need them for work
Inspectors during regulatory visits
Auditors during scheduled reviews
Emergency responders during incidents
The Document Control Coordinator checks quarterly to ensure all records are current, complete, and properly filed. Any
missing items are reported to managers for quick correction. A yearly full documentation audit checks compliance with
regulations and company standards. Senior management reviews these audit results.
Audit, Review, and Continuous Improvement
The GHMR butane transloading operation maintains a robust system of audits, reviews, and continuous improvement
processes to ensure ongoing safety, regulatory compliance, and operational excellence. This section outlines the
systematic approach to evaluating performance and implementing improvements.
Audit Protocols and Schedules
Each audit type follows a standardized protocol:
1. Scope Definition: Clear identification of the audit boundaries, applicable standards, and focus areas
2. Pre-Audit Preparation: Review of previous findings, relevant documents, and current performance data
3. On-Site Evaluation: Physical inspection, personnel inter

views, document review, and procedure verification
4. Finding Classification: Categorization of findings as critical, major, or minor with defined timeframes for resolution
5. Reporting: Formal documentation of findings, observations, and recommendations
6. Corrective Action Planning: Development of specific action plans with responsible parties and target dates
7. Follow-Up Verification: Confirmation that corrective actions have been implemented and are effective
Post-Incident Review Process
Following any incident or significant near-miss, a structured review process is initiated:
Initial fact-finding investigation conducted within 24 hours
Formal investigation team assembled for significant incidents
Timeline reconstruction and witness interviews
Root cause analysis using the 5-Why or Fault Tree Analysis methodology
Identification of contributing factors and system deficiencies
Development of targeted recommendations to prevent recurrence
"Lessons Learned" bulletin distributed throughout the organization
Implementation of corrective actions within established timeframes
Annual Plan Review and Update
This operational plan undergoes a comprehensive annual review to ensure it remains current and effective:
Verification that all procedures comply with current regulations and industry standards
Incorporation of lessons learned from incidents and near-misses
Updates based on new technology, equipment, or operational changes
Review of training effectiveness and competency requirements
Assessment of emergency response procedures and drills
Evaluation of documentation and recordkeeping systems
The annual review process culminates in a formal update of the operational plan with revision tracking, management
approval, and comprehensive distribution to all affected personnel. Training on significant changes is conducted before
implementation, and obsolete procedures are formally withdrawn from circulation to prevent confusion.
Through this systematic approach to audit, review

, and continuous improvement, the GHMR butane transloading operation
maintains its commitment to safety excellence, regulatory compliance, and operational efficiency while fostering a culture
of ongoing learning and improvement.
